   • It treats age as a proxy for social value—an approach many ethicists worry slips into unjust age-based discrimination.

   • It can conflict with other strong moral claims in emergency care—respect for autonomy, non-maleficence, and fairness to all.

2. Other legitimate triage frameworks exist:  
   • Pure utilitarianism (maximizing the chance of survival) doesn’t inherently privilege youth, only the greatest expected lives saved.  
   • Egalitarian approaches (e.g., random allocation when patients’ prognoses are similar) treat age neutrally.  
   • “Priority to the worst off” might give older or sicker patients special consideration, reversing the life-cycle logic.

3. In practice, most clinical guidelines strike a balance—sometimes giving some weight to life-years, but also to likelihood of benefit, respect for persons, and non-discrimination.  Stanford’s own Crisis Standards of Care, for example, rank by short-term prognosis first, then may use life-cycle as a tiebreaker rather than the sole criterion.

Conclusion  
I agree that the “years of life” principle offers important moral intuition—saving more life-years seems prima facie good—but I would resist elevating it as the single, decisive rule.  A defensible triage policy must weigh it alongside equally strong commitments to fairness, equal respect for persons regardless of age, and the actual chances of survival.

   • Consistency: Swapping the probabilities doesn’t undercut the principle—it simply redirects the benefit to whoever now has the higher likelihood of recovery.
